module_introduction.text:
Welcome to the final module! This lesson is on Auxiliaries, or 'helper verbs'. These are small but very powerful words like do, does, did, have, and is. They "help" main verbs to form questions and negative sentences.

This is a very common error for Francophone students. Why? Because French has different ways to ask questions (like "Est-ce que...") and make negatives ("ne...pas"). English must use an auxiliary verb like 'do'. For example, to make "I like" negative, you cannot say "I like not...". You must say "I do not like...". To ask "You like?", you must say "Do you like...?". This module will teach you the correct pattern for do, does, did, and have, which will make your English much more accurate.

contrastive_explanation.text:
Let's look at how English "helper" verbs are different from French.

Do / Does / Did in Negatives:

The Rule: To make a negative sentence in the Present Simple, you must use do not (don't) or does not (doesn't). For the Past Simple, you must use did not (didn't). The auxiliary is always followed by the base verb (the infinitive without 'to', 's', or 'ed').

Examples: "I don't know." "He doesn't speak..." "They didn't go..."

French Connection: French uses "ne...pas" around the main verb ("Je ne sais pas." "Il ne parle pas.").

The Error: Students translate this logic directly. They either add "not" after the verb (❌ "He speaks not...") or forget the auxiliary completely. You must use do, does, or did.

Important Exception: The verb 'to be' (am/is/are/was/were) does not use 'do'. We say "I am not" (not "I do not be"), "He is not" (not "He does not be").

Do / Does / Did in Questions:

The Rule: To ask a simple "yes/no" question in the Present Simple, you must start with Do or Does. For the Past Simple, you must start with Did.

Pattern: (Auxiliary) + Subject + Verb (base)?

Examples: "Do you live here?" "Does Ngono cook well?" "Did you finish?"

French Connection: French uses "Est-ce que..." (e.g., "Est-ce qu'il parle...?") or inverts the main verb ("Parle-t-il...?"). Most commonly, spoken French just uses a rising voice ("Tu aimes...?").

The Error: Students use the spoken French style: ❌ "You like football?". This is not a correct question in English.

Important Exception: The verb 'to be' does not use 'do' for questions either. We say "Are you ready?" (not "Do you be ready?").

Have / Has (as Auxiliaries):

The Rule: 'Have' and 'has' are used as auxiliary verbs to form the Present Perfect tense (actions connecting the past to the present).

Examples: "I have eaten." "She has finished her work."

French Connection: This is very similar to the passé composé, which uses 'avoir' or 'être' as the auxiliary! ("J'ai mangé." "Elle a fini.")

The Error: Because the passé composé is so common, students overuse the Present Perfect in English (see Category 1). The auxiliary errors here are:

• Agreement: Forgetting that 'he/she/it' uses 'has' (❌ "He have gone").
• Questions: Forgetting to invert the auxiliary and the subject (❌ "You have seen it?" ➡️ ✅ "Have you seen it?").

Note about 'have' as a main verb: When 'have' means possession ("I have a car"), it is NOT an auxiliary—it is the main verb. In this case, it needs 'do' to form negatives and questions: "I don't have a car." "Do you have a car?"

common_errors.correct: I do not (don't) know the answer.
common_errors.french_connection: A direct translation of "Je ne sais pas...". English must use the auxiliary 'do' for a negative.

common_errors.correct: My sister does not (doesn't) like fufu.
common_errors.french_connection: "Ma sœur n'aime pas...". In English, the subject 'sister' (she) requires the auxiliary 'does'.

common_errors.wrong: We went not to the market yesterday.
common_errors.correct: We did not (didn't) go to the market yesterday.
common_errors.french_connection: French "Nous ne sommes pas allés...". Students add 'not' to the past verb. English must use 'didn't' + the base form ('go'), not 'went'.
This error (using 'no' as a verb negator) comes from simplifying "ne...pas" to just "no".
This is the common, informal French question structure: "Tu habites à Yaoundé?". English must use the auxiliary 'Do'.
"Il parle anglais?" or "Est-ce qu'il parle...". English must use the auxiliary 'Does' for a 'he/she/it' subject.
"Qu'est-ce que tu as dit?". Students forget the past auxiliary 'did' and fail to invert (What + did + you + say).
Subject-verb agreement. 'My friend' (he or she) must pair with 'has'. "Mon ami a...".
"Tu as mangé...?". English questions must invert the subject ('you') and the auxiliary ('have').

common_errors.wrong: My parents have not a taxi.
common_errors.correct: My parents do not have a taxi.
common_errors.french_connection: "Mes parents n'ont pas...". This is tricky. Here, 'have' is the MAIN verb (showing possession), not an auxiliary. When 'have' means possession, it needs 'do' as the auxiliary to make negatives: 'do not have'.

form_a_questions.question_text: My father ___ work in Douala; he works in Yaoundé.
form_a_questions.feedback: Correct! The subject is 'My father' (he). To make a negative in the Present Simple, we must use 'doesn't' (does not).

form_a_questions.question_text: We ___ have much money for the bendskin.
form_a_questions.feedback: Good job. The subject is 'We'. To make a negative in the Present Simple, we use 'don't' (do not).

form_a_questions.question_text: I ___ Muna at the market yesterday.
form_a_questions.feedback: Perfect! For a negative in the past ('yesterday'), we must use 'didn't' + base verb ('see'). "Didn't saw" is a common error, but it's incorrect.

form_a_questions.question_text: Find the error: "He speaks not French."
form_a_questions.feedback: You found it! This error comes from the French "Il ne parle pas...". In English, we must use the auxiliary 'does': "He does not speak...".

form_a_questions.question_text: ___ you live near the school compound?
form_a_questions.feedback: Yes! To ask a simple question in the Present Simple with the subject 'you', we must start with 'Do'. Asking "You live...?" is a common error from French spoken style.
Correct! The subject is 'the lesson' (it). For a question with 'it', we must use the auxiliary 'does'.

form_a_questions.question_text: ___ you go to church last Sunday?
form_a_questions.feedback: That's right. The time is "last Sunday" (finished past). We must use the past auxiliary 'Did' to ask the question.

form_a_questions.question_text: Find the error: "Why you look so tired?"
form_a_questions.feedback: Good catch! This comes from the French "Pourquoi tu sembles...". English questions need an auxiliary: "Why do you look...".
Correct! The subject 'My brother' (he) must use the auxiliary 'has' to form the Present Perfect tense (like French "Il a fini").
Yes! To ask a question about life experience, we use the Present Perfect auxiliary 'Have'. We must invert it with the subject: "Have you...".

form_b_questions.question_text: This old phone ___ work very well.
form_b_questions.feedback: Correct! The subject is 'This old phone' (it). To make a negative in the Present Simple, we must use 'doesn't' (does not).

form_b_questions.question_text: They ___ sell beignets in that shop.
form_b_questions.feedback: Good job! The subject is 'They'. To make a negative in the Present Simple, we use 'don't' (do not).
Perfect! For a negative in the past ('last night'), we must use 'didn't' + base verb ('do'). "Didn't did" is incorrect.

form_b_questions.question_text: Find the error: "I like not this hot weather."
form_b_questions.feedback: You found it! This error comes from French "ne...pas" structure. In English, we must use the auxiliary 'do': "I do not like...".
Yes! To ask a simple question in the Present Simple with the subject 'your parents' (they), we must start with 'Do'.
Correct! The subject is 'your mother' (she). For a question with 'she', we must use the auxiliary 'does'.
That's right! The time is "this morning" (finished past). We must use the past auxiliary 'Did' to ask the question.
Good catch! This comes from French "Qu'est-ce qu'il a dit?". English questions need the auxiliary 'did' and we must invert: "What did he say?".
Correct! The subject 'The students' (they) must use the auxiliary 'have' to form the Present Perfect tense.

form_b_questions.question_text: Find the error: "You have finished your chores?"
form_b_questions.feedback: You spotted it! This comes from French "Tu as fini...?". English questions must invert the subject ('you') and the auxiliary ('have'): "Have you finished...?".
